description: Bell-shaped relic stupa on a stepped square terrace, tapering through stacked rings to a slender gilded finial spire.

image.prompt:
Product photograph of one isolated object, shot from a HIGH THREE-QUARTER ANGLE: the camera is well above the object and tilted down about 30 degrees, so the top of the object is clearly visible along with its front and one side. Not a straight-on elevation.

The object: Bell-shaped relic stupa rising from a stepped square terrace, rounded bell drum above a set of receding square plinths, a stack of narrowing horizontal rings above the bell tapering to a long slender needle finial, small niched alcove on each face of the base Materials: Whitewashed lime plaster crazed and flaking to grey render beneath, gilded finial with tarnished dull patches, dark rain streaking down the bell, moss in the terrace joints.

Form: build the object from a few simple, chunky, closed volumes. Prefer solid panels over lattice, mesh, grilles or perforated screens; keep any openings few, large and clearly separated. No thin spindly protrusions, no wires, no chains, no fringes, no lace, no fine filigree, no dense repeated slots or cut-outs. Keep the silhouette simple and readable from every side. Keep the object's SHAPE simple; richness must come from the surface finish, wear and materials rather than from intricate geometry. The object is still photoreal and highly detailed in its texture -- only its form is simple.

Framing: long-lens near-orthographic perspective, minimal foreshortening. The object is perfectly centred and occupies about 75% of the frame height, with clear empty margin on all four sides. The whole object is in frame; nothing is cropped.

Background: completely flat seamless neutral 50% grey (#808080). The object floats in empty space against an infinite seamless backdrop, photographed as a cut-out with nothing underneath it. There is no surface for it to rest on and nothing for it to cast a shadow onto. No floor, no ground plane, no horizon line, no cast shadow, no contact shadow, no reflection, no vignette, no gradient.

Lighting: flat even studio illumination from all sides, soft and shadowless, like a lightbox. No strong key light, no rim light, no coloured light, no specular blowout, no dramatic highlights. Colours must read as true albedo.

One object only, nothing else in frame. No people, no hands, no other props, no packaging, no text, no labels, no watermarks, no measurement annotations, no arrows, no borders, no drop shadow.

Photoreal, sharp focus edge to edge, clean and undamaged geometry, realistic materials and surface wear. Not stylised, not cartoon, not low-poly, not a 3D render preview, not a wireframe.

license.notice: Fully synthetic. No third-party scanned or scraped geometry.

review.critique: FINAL VERDICT (rebuild). Overall visual fidelity 0.87 -- not a pass self-score. 5,184/16,000 triangles, 7/12 draw calls, 4/8 materials, 7/32 unique geometries, 2 canvas textures.

featureReviews.evidence: Envelope built at exactly 8.00 x 14.00 x 8.00 m against the declared 8 x 14 x 8. Area-weighted band comparison against the Meshy reference (scratch/_mon/bands.mjs) gives mean |delta width| 0.019 and |delta depth| 0.019 of height with no band past 0.045; the first build measured 0.030 with the spire bands 6-8 at +0.06, now within 0.017.
featureReviews.notes: The bell shoulder and harmika are now read off the proxy at 56 slices (scratch/_mon/profile.mjs) rather than off the foreshortened three-quarter plate. Residuals: band 3 (the foot mouldings and lower body) is +0.04 of height, where the 2.70 m rings sit 0.07 outside the proxy's 2.63; band 5 (the shoulder) +0.03. Meshy reads the plate 14% taller than declared; the declared 14 m still wins.

featureReviews.evidence: Bell as one lathe: foot mouldings at 2.70, a body from r 2.36 at 4.52 to 1.98 at 6.45, a quarter-ellipse shoulder rounding over to a flat 1.30 m crown at 7.72, the harmika block standing on the flat with a 0.75 m neck running up inside it. Harmika 2.10 / 1.52 m square from 7.55 to 9.05, a metre-tall lower block seated down into the crown; spire from r 0.66 at 8.99 to 0.22 at 12.30, sixteen rings; closed gilt needle with a bud.
featureReviews.notes: The first build's bell was a quarter-cosine from the foot -- an OGIVE, full at the haunch and pointed at the top -- and it stopped at 8.30 with the harmika starting at 8.55, a 0.25 m air gap under a floating block. The proxy's radius-by-height says what a bell is: near-vertical flanks (2.36 at 4.1, 2.03 at 5.1, 1.90 at 6.4 in 14 m scale) that round over the top 1.3 m to a 0.72 neck, with a 1.66 m harmika on the neck. A quarter-ellipse shoulder was tried first and put band 5 at +0.07 -- a hemisphere, not a domed cone -- and the proxy's own normalised falloff (0.93, 0.85, 0.69, 0.44, 0.17) was fitted instead. The harmika, at 2.56 m in the first build, was read off the plate's diagonal and was 50% too wide; the spire base at 1.05 was what put bands 6-8 a twentieth of the height too fat. The lever remains the LATHE: the neck is two more profile points, not a mesh, and the prop is still 7 draw calls.

featureReviews.evidence: Six redented slabs from y=0.00 to 3.85 as one merged extrusion, with four arched aedicules standing 0.30 m proud and dark back panels 0.23 m behind their front plane. Unchanged in this round apart from the lichen tile.
featureReviews.notes: Two things here were learned by rebuilding. Each slab is an EXTRUSION of a closed redented plan rather than a wide box crossed by a deep one: crossed boxes put their top faces in the same plane facing the same way over the whole intersection and z-fight, while one closed plan has no interior coincidence at all. And the arch aperture was first written as an arc from PI to 0, which swept through the BOTTOM of the circle: the arch head was left filled solid with the arc's own seam z-fighting across it, giving a square window with a ghost arch drawn on it. The direction of a half-circle is not a detail on this prop; it is the feature. The niche storey was also re-proportioned to 1.70 m so a 1.45 m aedicule fits inside it -- sized the other way round, the arch head ran up through the cornice above and was swallowed.

featureReviews.evidence: Four materials at PBR confidence 0.734-0.860, all measured, all textureless to the generator; two post-construction Canvas 2D wear tiles bound as map and bumpMap on the stucco and the stone, every tone a measured ratio against the clean surface beside it on the plate.
featureReviews.notes: The first build shipped flat paint and called the plate's peeling 'wear below the resolvable band'; it is the bell's identity at any distance, and it is now authored. Stucco: exposed lime render at (0.754, 0.738, 0.703) of the clean whitewash, drips at 0.703, between-flake mottle at 0.90, a 640-walk crack network, and dark render cores measured at 0.483 but SHIPPED at 0.62 because the bell's shaded flank renders near luma 120 and 0.483 of that is the backdrop's 58, which the silhouette gate reads as a hole. Stone: lichen crust as a yellow shift (blue at 0.86, pale channels held near 1.0 because a multiplier cannot brighten) and moss at (0.86, 0.85, 0.72). Discs scattered about a centre rendered as polka dots on the first attempt; the flakes are random walks of overlapping discs filled once as a union. The whitewash is still #A7A7A1 and the terrace #9E9B91 -- the tiles only ever multiply them -- and the finial stays worn ochre. Factory 80 ms, 2.7 MB texture VRAM, no per-pixel JavaScript.

name: Chedi
notes: Vertically the tallest thing in a village skyline, so the readable feature is the profile: stepped square base, rounded bell, ringed taper, needle spire. That silhouette must survive at distance where no surface detail is visible at all. Collider is a cylinder rather than the building-part default box because the bell and spire are round in plan and a box proxy would leave a player colliding with empty air at the corners. Declared at 14 m, above the building-part category's 8 m prior, which is correct for a village chedi -- a monastery one is far larger still. No destruction groups: it is static landmark geometry.
